title: Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014
short_title: Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would deregulate university fees and let the government fund more student places.
Universities and private colleges could set their own tuition fees, and the government would subsidise places for diplomas and associate degrees as well as bachelor degrees.
Providers with 500 or more government-funded places would have to spend 20 per cent of extra revenue on scholarships for disadvantaged students.
changes: Extends demand-driven funding to sub-bachelor qualifications and private providers.
Requires large providers to put 20 per cent of additional revenue into a Commonwealth Scholarship Scheme.
Changes the HELP loan programme, including a new minimum repayment threshold and removal of loan fees.
Allows universities to charge research students tuition fees up to a maximum set by course cost.
Makes technical amendments to the Australian Research Council Act 2001 for Future Fellowships.
summary.affected: Universities, private higher education providers, and students.

divisions.question: Christopher Pyne It is my great pleasure to sum up the debate on the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014. I would like to thank all of my colleagues, particularly on this side of the House, who have given passionate and informed speeches about this reform bill over the course of the last week and a half of sittings. I thank those members of the opposition who have also participated, although I would not say their speeches were nearly as well informed as the ones from the side of the House, because they are not supporting the higher education reform bill. They are putting their head deeply in the sand and refusing to acknowledge the need for reform in higher education. It has been a very long debate. Most members of the government have participated in it. I thank my colleagues for doing this process a second time, for the second reform bill. It is because the government believes so fervently in these reforms that it has brought the bill back. The reform bill amends the Higher Education Support Act 2003 and the Australian Research Council Act 2001 to implement a fair, balanced and essential set of reforms to Australia's higher education and research system. The reform bill represents the boldest ambitions for Australian higher education in generations. It aims to make it possible for Australia to develop the best higher education system in the world. Above all, this will enable our students to get an education of the quality they need and deserve in this world of intensifying international competition. It will do so while making Australian higher education more equitable, affordable and accessible than ever before. This is the right package at the right time for Australian universities and colleges. More importantly, it is the best package for students. It has been designed thoughtfully and deliberately following careful review, consideration and consultation. All the higher education peak bodies around Australia support the core elements of these reforms.
Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014 - Third Reading - Pass the bill
Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea

speeches.speaker: Bill Shorten
speeches.brief: Moved to suspend standing orders to condemn the Prime Minister over plans for $100,000 university degrees, noting the Senate had voted against the proposal the previous night, and called on the government to bring the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill on for debate so parliament could reject it again.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Introduced a revised Higher Education and Research Reform Bill after the Senate rejected the previous version, withdrawing the proposal to index HECS debts to the 10-year Treasury bond rate and adding an indexation pause for primary carers of children under five, while saying the reforms would let an extra 80,000 students a year access Commonwealth support by 2018.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Defended reintroducing the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, arguing Labor's $6.6 billion cut to universities left them needing to replace lost revenue, and proposed students pay 50 per cent of education costs instead of the current 40 per cent, with taxpayers covering the remaining 50 rather than 60 per cent.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Opposed the higher education bill as a repeat of previously rejected policy, said the government spent $15 million advertising a package already defeated in the Senate, and cited Queensland University of Technology figures showing business students would be charged 88 per cent of their degree's cost, far above the government's claimed 50 per cent student contribution.

speeches.speaker: Ann Sudmalis
speeches.brief: Backed the bill, said voting it down risked 1,700 technical and support jobs and funding for 35,000 researchers, detailed $150 million for national research infrastructure and $26 million for dementia research, and noted only three out of 20 people in her Gilmore electorate attend university against youth unemployment exceeding 50 per cent in some villages.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Voiced support for the higher education bill for the second time, accusing Labor of running a shameful scaremongering campaign to defeat overdue reform benefiting disadvantaged and regional students.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Backed the higher education bill, citing Dobell's average family income of $1,294 a week against the New South Wales average of $1,477, noted only 50 per cent of Dobell students attain a Year 12 qualification, and said the Central Coast and Hunter districts face a shortfall of 7,600 university places that a new local university precinct could address.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, saying the government's total higher education cuts amount to $5 billion despite an election promise of 'no cuts to education', and cited Universities Australia modelling that course fees would need to rise 58 per cent for engineering and science and 110 per cent for environmental studies to offset the funding cuts.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Backed the bill, said HECS has applied since 1989 and Labor cut $6.6 billion from tertiary education in 2012 to 2013, and detailed new Commonwealth support for 48,000 diploma students costing $371 million and 35,000 bachelor students at non-university providers costing $449 million.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill's $1.9 billion in university cuts and $100,000 degrees, said the government spent more than $14 million advertising the reforms, and contrasted the University of Newcastle's 24 per cent low socioeconomic-status enrolment with 8.5 per cent at the University of New South Wales and seven per cent at the University of Sydney.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Accused Labor of hypocrisy for cutting $6.6 billion from higher education before opposing this reform, said graduates earn 75 per cent, or roughly a million dollars, more over their lifetimes than non-graduates, and noted former Labor figures John Dawkins, Gareth Evans and Maxine McKew have all backed the government's plan.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, noting 39 coalition MPs voted for a blank leadership option in this week's spill, said the bill still cuts $1.9 billion from universities, and cited National Tertiary Education Union modelling showing average degrees could cost $40,000 to $65,000, with medical degrees reaching $180,000.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, citing University of Western Australia analysis that rural and regional students attend university at about 60 per cent of the rate of their metropolitan counterparts, and that about 50 per cent of rural students who receive offers defer them to meet financial independence requirements for Austudy.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, recalling that the previous version of the bill cut $5.8 billion from higher education, criticised a $15 million government advertising campaign for the changes, and said the current bill still cuts $1.9 billion from Australian universities.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill with amendments, said the cost of a country student living away from home can reach $20,000 a year for a family, noted La Trobe University's Mildura campus will cap fee increases at 10 per cent so a degree there will cost about $16,000, and said HECS repayments only begin once graduates earn over $50,000 a year.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, criticised an $8.5 million government advertising campaign for changes that have not even passed parliament, cited Bond University's uncapped law degree costing $127,000 as evidence of what deregulation could bring, and said Universities Australia figures show an environmental science degree would need a 110 per cent fee increase to offset the funding cuts.

speeches.speaker: Darren Chester
speeches.brief: Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, noted the previous Labor government cut $6.6 billion from higher education while in office, said the reforms are backed by organisations including Universities Australia and the Group of Eight, and credited Senator Bridget McKenzie's Senate committee for gathering input from university vice-chancellors.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014 for its benefits to her Durack electorate, highlighting the Geraldton Universities Centre, established in 2002 and reconstituted as a cooperative model in 2010, which has graduated more than 200 students with around 200 currently enrolled, and noted providers with more than 500 Commonwealth supported places must invest 20 per cent of new revenue in scholarships for disadvantaged students.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, saying the government has already given up $3.5 billion of its original $3.9 billion in savings yet the bill still contains $1.9 billion in cuts to universities and $100,000 degrees, and warned the University of Newcastle alone would lose $153 million over three years.

speeches.speaker: Matt Williams
speeches.brief: Continued supporting the higher education reforms, noting Singapore's High Commissioner said one in 30 Singaporeans had studied in Australia, citing notable graduates including Singapore's President Dr Tony Tan Keng Yam, who completed a PhD in Mathematics at the University of Adelaide, and said Australian education exports contribute around $15 billion a year.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, saying it contains more than $2 billion in cuts to higher education, and cited Bond University in Western Australia as evidence that fee deregulation will push some degrees above $100,000.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Supported the higher education reforms, citing a 16 per cent decline in international education enrolments, down 130,000 since 2009 under the previous government, and pointed to published 2016 fees from the Queensland University of Technology and University of Western Australia as evidence against $100,000 degree claims.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Supported the higher education reforms, saying students will receive a 50 per cent taxpayer-funded gift toward their degree and only start repaying once earning $50,000, and cited estimates that university graduates earn 75 per cent higher incomes over their lifetime, equivalent to $1 million in additional earnings.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, noting the government's own claimed savings have shrunk from over $4 billion to $400 million over the forward estimates, and itemised nearly $2 billion in cuts including $171 million from equity programs and $80 million from the Australian Research Council.
